node.title: Re: Perlsecret - plus no-ops (updated)
node.author: haukex
node.doctext:
with a note of : (The + is in the above line is a no-op, used to tell grep that the parentheses are not enclosing its arguments.) what does that note actually mean?

If [doc://grep] is immediately followed by an opening parenthesis, that parenthesis would be interpreted as starting the argument list of [doc://grep], so for example grep( /foo/, @array ) or grep( {$_>123} @array ). However, in this case, the expression being used to search the list is "()=@$_". One could write this in the grep BLOCK LIST form of [doc://grep] as grep {()=@$_} @arrays, however, in this case the author has chosen the grep EXPR, LIST form of [doc://grep]. But if one wrote grep ()=@$_, @arrays, then Perl would think that you were calling [doc://grep] with no arguments ("grep()"), followed by "=@$_, @arrays", which is invalid syntax. Therefore, to tell Perl that the parentheses are actually not introducing the arguments of [doc://grep], one has to disambiguate and add the + operator. Because in this case it has no effect except informing the Perl parser, it is in that sense a no-op. Another way to disambiguate the situation would have been an extra pair of parentheses, as in grep( ()=@$_, @arrays ).

This is one of the reasons that I perfer the BLOCK LIST forms of [doc://grep] and [doc://map], and the same issue with parentheses commonly comes up in the arguments to [doc://print].

Typo fix in the last sentence.

Update: In this case, the use of the "Saturn" [doc://perlsecret#Goatse|"secret"] operator doesn't even really make sense, since all that is being done is that empty array references are being filtered out. This could be written as grep {@$_} @arrays (or grep @$_, @arrays), or if one wanted to be explicit that one is filtering on the number of elements the arrays contain, e.g. grep {0+@$_} @arrays.
